doc.title: Alan Raph interviewed by Monk Rowe, Danbury, Connecticut, November 20, 2001

title: Occupation, daughter, and bass trombone
summary: Raph says he is a musician and music teacher, and talks about his ten-year-old daughter's piano and flute and his second family. He names bass trombone as his main instrument.

story.theme_name: Meeting, marrying and raising a family
story.community_name: Talking about my children and grandchildren

blocks.x: We are filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in Danbury, Connecticut. I’m pleased to have Alan Raph with me today. I’m wondering, what do you put on your income tax form as your occupation?
That covers a lot of things for you, doesn’t it?
Yeah. I put musician, slash — well for my wife and I — musician, music teacher, but it goes both ways.
What does your daughter think? You have a ten year old?
I have a ten year old, yes.
Does she have a sense of what you do?

Sort of. She has a sense of what I do now which is somewhat different than what I did let’s say twenty years ago, because I had a long life before she came along. And I have two kids that are actually older than me at this point you know. I have a 43-year-old and I have a 36-year-old, a couple of grandkids in California.
Wow. So you have kind of a whole second career.

Yeah. Second family, second life. What does she think? She knows of course that I’m a musician, she knows that I conduct the Danbury Brass Band because she’s been to many concerts, she knows that I teach around here, I teach right now at the moment at the Emmanuel Lutheran School, I do a couple of hours a week there teaching general music, which I asked for rather than trombone or instruments or that. And she knows that I sit with her every morning for an hour and she practices piano, which we did this morning included. She has been playing for five years and she’s got a remarkably good ear and a good musical sense and she has her struggles are more with reading notes. That is where we kind of have to pound things into her. But she’s getting there.
Yeah. Does she like to improvise a little bit?

Very little. She’s not sure what it is. But just recently — she is singing in a choir on Sundays. And they’re going to give a concert. And the choir director brought out a particular piece of music that has a flute solo at the beginning and he said well if anybody plays flute or recorder or tin whistle or anything, audition for it and we’ll have you play the solo. So she asked me to borrow a flute, which I did from one of the guys in the Brass Band, and she practiced it, and she’d been playing for a week and a half and she played the solo and the guy said okay. So she came home, she said, “I got the gig.”
All right. She’s getting the terms down.

She’s getting the terms down. She’s got a good sense of humor. And her mother of course is a musician. My wife is a string player. So between strings and brass, of course naturally she’s going to gravitate toward the woodwinds. For new expenses.
Sure. So you have to pay somebody else to give the lessons?

A trombone player primarily. Bass trombone specifically, although I play related instruments, tenor and baritone horn and tuba. I’ve done a lot of work on the other instruments too. But basically I guess my reputation is bass trombone. I’ve been doing that for some years.
